$comment: Controlled vocabulary of skeletal and soft-tissue attachment sites. Every `attachments` reference in data/muscles-*.json resolves to an `id` here. Three things this buys that a free-string list did not: (1) `partOf` gives the bone-first browse a drill-down (pectoral girdle -> scapula -> acromion); (2) `presence` records where an element is absent, so the interface can show that a muscle's attachment had to move rather than silently dropping the row; (3) `correlate: true` marks sites that leave a recognisable osteological trace, which is the entry point for fossil reconstruction. Presence statements are sourced; where a source is not yet attached the claim is standard comparative anatomy and flagged `sourced: false`.

presence.note: A therian novelty. Incipient in monotremes, which is why the monotreme shoulder is the readable intermediate: it divides the ancestral supracoracoideus field into supraspinatus and infraspinatus.
Cartilaginous dorsal extension of the scapula. Its loss in mammals shifts several axio-appendicular insertions onto the scapular border itself.

All that remains of the coracoid in therians, fused to the scapula. Muscles that arose from the coracoid bone in other tetrapods — biceps brachii and coracobrachialis — arise from this process instead.

Lost as an independent ossification in therians, surviving only as the coracoid process of the scapula. This single loss forces the origin of the supracoracoideus onto the lateral scapula and removes the coracoid head of the subcoracoscapularis — the clearest case in the dataset of an attachment moving because its bone disappeared.
Carries the origin of the procoracohumeralis — the amphibian name for what amniotes call the deltoideus clavicularis. The muscle is renamed for the bone, not for any change in the muscle.
Dermal element linking the pectoral girdle to the skull in fishes. Its loss along the tetrapod stem is what frees the girdle from the head and permits a neck.
Reduced or absent in many cursorial mammals; fused into the furcula in birds.
Retained in monotremes, which is a large part of why the monotreme pectoralis has a more extensive origin than the therian one.

Carries both the pectoralis and the supracoracoideus. The whole flight apparatus is powered from below the centre of mass because the supracoracoideus tendon is redirected dorsally through the foramen triosseum.

The single most useful osteological correlate in the pectoral appendage. Its presence and shape is the primary evidence for reconstructing the pectoralis, supracoracoideus and deltoid complex in fossil taxa.
Common origin of the extensor (dorsal-mass, radial-innervated) forearm musculature throughout Tetrapoda.

Common origin of the flexor (ventral-mass) forearm musculature. Diogo & Molnar (2014) follow Sigurdsen & Bolt (2009) in reidentifying the salamander 'ulnar condyle' of Francis (1934) as the entepicondyle.
Insertion of the triceps throughout Tetrapoda; a reliable fossil indicator of elbow extensor leverage.

Expansion of the iliac blade along the synapsid stem tracks the enlargement of the iliofemoralis/gluteal field and is central to Bishop & Pierce's (2024) argument that erect posture was acquired late.

The best single fossil-muscle landmark in the vertebrate skeleton. It carries the caudofemoralis, so its size reads directly as femoral-retractor power, and its independent reduction in birds and loss in mammals marks two separate departures from tail-driven locomotion.
Independently acquired in birds and mammals; a sesamoid in the knee extensor tendon.
Proximal tibial crest receiving the knee extensor tendon; prominent in archosaurs.
No tetrapod counterpart. The tetrapod autopod is a novelty rather than a transformed radial series — see Diogo et al. (2016) on the distal tendon primordium.
Replaced by the urostyle in anurans and shortened to the pygostyle in birds — both associated with caudofemoralis reduction.
Cartilaginous plate in the fenestra ovalis. Target of the opercularis, a pectoral-girdle muscle that inserts on the ear — the amphibian substrate-vibration pathway.
Configuration of the temporal openings constrains adductor mandibulae volume and orientation; the primary osteological handle on jaw muscle reconstruction in fossils.
Incorporated into the mammalian middle ear as the incus.
Transformed into the stapes in tetrapods; the depressor hyomandibulae becomes the stapedius, keeping arch 2 identity and CN VII innervation throughout.
The reduced first (mandibular) gill slit. Its pouch is the ancestor of the tympanic cavity, and the region keeps trigeminal innervation throughout.

Cartilage at the corner of the mouth carrying the levator anguli oris. In colubroid snakes it is elaborated into the venom gland, which is why parts of the levator anguli oris there insert on the gland rather than the plate.
Rostral origin of the adductor internus in anurans, medial to the eye.
Tendinous sheet receiving much of the adductor complex in turtles.
Endoskeletal pectoral girdle of fishes, bearing the articular process for the fin. It is the element that becomes the separate scapula and coracoid of tetrapods.
The fin articulation on the scapulocoracoid. Diogo et al. (2016) use it as the landmark separating dorsal (adductor) from ventral (abductor) muscle origins — the fish equivalent of the glenoid.
Ramus of the fish pelvic plate. Diogo et al. (2016) record several pelvic fin muscles arising from its dorsal, medial and caudolateral faces.
The proximo-distal series of the metapterygial axis. Its first and second elements correspond to the tetrapod stylopod and zeugopod; the pronator and supinator series attach segmentally along it.
Principal origin surface for the adductor mandibulae in taxa with an open or emarginated temporal region.
The sole bone of the therian lower jaw; elsewhere one of several, with the postdentary series carrying part of the adductor insertion.
Major adductor insertion surface in non-mammalian tetrapods.
Incorporated into the mammalian middle ear or lost as the dentary takes over the jaw joint.
Forms the jaw joint with the quadrate in non-mammals; becomes the malleus in mammals, which is why the mammalian jaw joint is squamosal-dentary instead.
Incorporated into the mammalian middle ear or lost as the dentary takes over the jaw joint.
